FACTS IN BOTH THE CASES 1.

Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that on 23.04.2019, at about 10:15 a.m, one lady namely Pooja Sharma along with her daughter Taniya @ Tannu were returning after a visit to Hedgewar hospital.

It has been alleged that when they both reached at Road No. 57, Near Honda Showroom,
Arjun Nagar, and while they both were crossing the road, a white car bearing registration no.
DL1ZA-5639 came from the side of Arjun Nagar at very high speed and hit the mother-dauther-duo.
It has been further alleged that the said vehicle was being driven by its driver i.e. R1 herein, rashly and negligently due to which the mother-daughter duo suffered injuries in their legs and arms.

Allegedly, the driver of the offending vehicle was apprehended by the public persons at the spot itself and both the injured ladies were thereon taken to Hedgewar hospital in the offending vehicle itself, where they received treatment for the injuries suffered by them before being discharged on the same day.
An FIR bearing no. 79/19, PS Jagatpuri thereafter came to be registered on the complaint of Ms. Pooja Sharma for the offences u/s 279/337 IPC against the driver of the offending vehicle.
Finally, two DAR's came to be filed in due course as there were two injured victims of the accident.
2. Copies of DAR petition were supplied to all the parties in due course of the proceedings.

Findings of the Tribunal are as follows:
Issue no.1 18.
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.

It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.

The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.

Reference in this regard can be made to the propositions of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bimla Devi & Ors. Vs Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors, reported in (2009) 13 SC 530, which were reiterated in MACT Nos. 269/19 & 270/19 Pooja Sharma Vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors.

sentences.text: In view of the medical records placed on record by the petitioners, no dispute is left regarding the injuries of the petitioners Tanya @ Tannu and Pooja Sharma in the above accident.
26. Section 168 of the Act enjoins the Claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable.
It has to be borne in mind that the compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
27. The case of Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343, is one of the most prominent judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court which deals with compensation in injuries cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar vs Ajay Kumar & Another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was held in this case that in routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under the heads-(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured , comprising (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment and (iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

Where the claimant suffers a permanent disability as a result of injuries, the assessment of compensation is also to be done under the head of loss of future earnings which would depend the effect and impact of such permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured.

The tribunal should not mechanically apply the percentage of permanent disability as the MACT Nos. 269/19 & 270/19 Pooja Sharma Vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors.
AND Taniya @ Tannu Vs. Suresh & Ors.
percentage of economic loss or loss of earning capacity.

entities.text: Pooja Sharma Vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: What requires to be assessed by the tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of percentage of the income.
It has to be quantified in terms of money to arrive at the future loss of earnings by applying standard multiplier method.
All injuries or permanent disabilities arising from injuries do not result in loss of earning capacity.

If there is no loss of employment or earning capacity, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of loss of future earnings, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities in consequent to his injuries.

On the other hand, it has been contended on behalf of R3 that the cheque given by the R2 towards insurance premium in respect of the offending vehicle was returned dishonoured and hence, it has been contended that the R3 had no liability to pay the compensation amount.
37.
The fact that the cheque Ex. R3W1/5 has been returned dishonoured has been duly proved on record by R3.

However, it is an admitted fact on record that the procedure in such cases as adopted by insurance company is that they give intimation to the owner as well as to the RTO as soon as the cheque is dishonoured.

The said fact has been specifically admitted by R3W1 during his cross-examination and the witness has further admitted that the intimation Ex. R3W1/6 and Ex.
R3W1/7 were given after about 11 months of the dishonoured of the cheque.

The said witness being an official of the R3 has further admitted during his cross examination that he has not placed any document on record in this case to show that the afore-said intimations were even sent.

Moreover,
the witness for the insurance company has also admitted that he has not placed on record any document to show that after dishonor of the premium cheque, there has never been any payment towards the premium of the policy in question.
Thus, the official witness of the insurance company has failed to rule out any part payment of the insurance premium in respect of the policy in question.

opennyai_summary.issue:
(i) Whether petitioner suffered injuries during the accident occurred on 23.04.2019 at about 10:15 am at Road no. 57, Honda Showroom, main road Arjun Nagar, Delhi within the jurisdiction of PS Jagatpuri, due to rash and negligent driving of the vehicle bearing no. DL-1ZA-5639 being driven by respondent no. 1/driver?
OPP. 
(ii) Whether petitioner is entitled for compensation, If so, to what extent and from whom?
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is tested on the touchstone of principle of preponderance of probabilities.
It is well settled that the procedure followed for proceedings conducted by an accident tribunal is similar to that followed by a civil court and in civil matters the facts are required to be established by preponderance of probabilities only and not by strict rules of evidence or beyond reasonable doubts as are required in a criminal prosecution.
The burden of proof in a civil case is never as heavy as that is required in a criminal case, but in a claim petition under the Motor Vehicles Act, this burden is infact even lesser than that in a civil case.
the subsequent judgment in the case of Parmeshwari Vs Amir Chand & Ors, 2011 (1) SCR 1906 (Civil Appeal No. 1082 of 2011) and also recently in another case Mangla Ram Vs. Oriental Insurance Co.
ltd. & Ors., 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
19.
(New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Washeema Bano (2022) SCC OnLine All 403 and Mangla Ram vs Oriental Insurance Company Ltd (2018) 5SCC 656).

If any party does not accept such charge-sheet, the burden must be on such party to adduce evidence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.
In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.
The tribunal should not mechanically apply the percentage of permanent disability as the MACT Nos. 269/19 & 270/19 Pooja Sharma Vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors.
AND Taniya @ Tannu Vs. Suresh & Ors.
percentage of economic loss or loss of earning capacity.
What requires to be assessed by the tribunal is the effect of the permanent disability on the earning capacity of the injured after assessing the loss of earning capacity in terms of percentage of the income.
It has to be quantified in terms of money to arrive at the future loss of earnings by applying standard multiplier method.
All injuries or permanent disabilities arising from injuries do not result in loss of earning capacity.
If there is no loss of employment or earning capacity, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of loss of future earnings, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities in consequent to his injuries.
Moreover,
the witness for the insurance company has also admitted that he has not placed on record any document to show that after dishonor of the premium cheque, there has never been any payment towards the premium of the policy in question.
Thus, the official witness of the insurance company has failed to rule out any part payment of the insurance premium in respect of the policy in question.
Such failure will thus render the insurance policy as merely a voidable contract as opposed to a contract void ab initio.
The fact that the intimation regarding dishonourment of the premium cheque has also been sent after a long delay of 11 months after dishonor of cheque by which time the accident had already taken place is a much delayed action on part of R3 to avoid the contract of insurance in this case.
Therefore, in view of the afore-said facts and circumstances and especially the failure on part of the insurance company in leading sufficient evidence to prove its contentions, the tribunal has no hesitation in hereby arriving at the finding that the liability to make the payment of compensation amount in both the cases is indeed of the R3 i.e. insurance company.
